subject: Mathematics
title: Rajesh's Treasure Map
hook: Rajesh uses a grid to locate a hidden treasure box at home, learning about the coordinate plane and how to find points.

characters.name: Rajesh
characters.role: class-7 student who loves treasure hunts

slides.title: Rajesh's Treasure Map
slides.storyContext: Grandmother hides a box in her house and gives Rajesh a grid to find it.

slides.title: The Treasure Hunt
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's grandmother loves games. She draws a grid on a piece of paper. 'Beta, this grid shows my house. The treasure is hidden at a specific spot. I will give you two clues: move 3 steps to the right and 2 steps up. That is where you must dig!' Rajesh looks confused. 'How do I translate that to the paper?' Grandmother smiles and teaches him coordinates.
slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate grid uses two numbers to describe exactly where a point is: one for right-left, one for up-down.

image.alt: The Treasure Hunt — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: What is a Coordinate?

points.text: A coordinate is a pair of numbers that pinpoints an exact location on a grid.
Think of it like an address: 'third floor, apartment 5B' tells you exactly where someone lives.
On a map, coordinates help rescue teams find lost hikers, or delivery people find your house.

slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate is like a home address but for points on a grid—it tells you exactly where to find something.

slides.title: The Coordinate Plane

points.text: A coordinate plane is a grid with two perpendicular lines: the x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical).
They meet at the origin (0, 0).
The x-axis goes left and right; the y-axis goes up and down.

example.problem: Name the axes of a coordinate plane.
example.solution: The horizontal axis is the x-axis. The vertical axis is the y-axis. They meet at the origin (0, 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: The coordinate plane is like a chessboard with horizontal and vertical lines that help you find exact locations.

slides.title: Rajesh Learns to Count
slides.storyContext: Rajesh stands at the center of the grid. Grandmother points. 'Do you see the middle point, where the lines cross? That is zero-zero, or the origin. Now, count 3 squares to the right. Then count 2 squares up. That is where the treasure is!' Rajesh carefully counts and marks the spot.
slides.inSimpleWords: Start at the center (origin), count right or left for the first number, count up or down for the second number.

slides.title: Ordered Pairs

points.text: A point on the coordinate plane is described by an ordered pair (x, y).
x is the horizontal distance from the origin (positive to the right, negative to the left).
y is the vertical distance from the origin (positive up, negative down).
The order matters: (3, 2) is different from (2, 3).

example.problem: Write the ordered pair for a point 4 units to the right and 3 units up from the origin.
example.solution: (4, 3). The first number is x (horizontal); the second is y (vertical).

slides.inSimpleWords: An ordered pair (x, y) tells you exactly how far right and how far up a point is.

slides.title: A Tricky Second Clue
slides.storyContext: Rajesh finds the first treasure and returns to Grandmother. 'Well done! Now here is a harder one. Imagine I moved some treasures left and down instead of right and up. If I say "3 steps left and 2 steps down," what would you write?' Rajesh thinks hard. 'Left is the opposite of right... and down is the opposite of up. So it would be negative!' Grandmother claps. 'Exactly! You are ready for negative coordinates.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Negative numbers on a coordinate plane mean going left or down from the origin.

slides.title: Positive and Negative Coordinates

points.text: Positive x: move right from the origin.
Negative x: move left from the origin.
Positive y: move up from the origin.
Negative y: move down from the origin.
Examples: (3, 2) is right-up; (−2, 4) is left-up; (−3, −2) is left-down.

example.problem: Write coordinates for a point 2 units left and 5 units down.
example.solution: (−2, −5). Left = negative x, down = negative y.

slides.inSimpleWords: Positive x and y go right and up. Negative x and y go left and down.

slides.title: Quadrants

points.text: The coordinate plane is divided into four quadrants by the axes.
Quadrant I: x positive, y positive (top-right).
Quadrant II: x negative, y positive (top-left).
Quadrant III: x negative, y negative (bottom-left).
Quadrant IV: x positive, y negative (bottom-right).

example.problem: In which quadrant is the point (−2, 3)?
example.solution: x is negative (−2), y is positive (3). This is Quadrant II (top-left).

slides.inSimpleWords: Each quadrant has a name based on whether x and y are positive or negative.

slides.title: Quadrants in the House
slides.storyContext: Grandmother divides her house into four sections using the middle point as the origin. 'The treasures are scattered in all four sections, beta. Some are in the front-right, some in the back-left, some below the floorboards. Each section is a quadrant. Your task is to find one treasure in each quadrant!' Rajesh grabs his pencil and begins mapping.
slides.inSimpleWords: A house divided by a center point creates four zones—just like the four quadrants on a coordinate plane.

slides.title: Naming Quadrants by Sign
slides.storyContext: Rajesh learns a trick to remember quadrants. Quadrant I is (+, +), Quadrant II is (−, +), Quadrant III is (−, −), and Quadrant IV is (+, −).

example.problem: List all four quadrants and their signs for x and y.

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember quadrants by their signs: top-right is both positive, top-left is x negative-y positive, and so on.

slides.title: Plotting Points

points.text: To plot a point (x, y), start at the origin.
Move right (positive x) or left (negative x) by x units.
Then move up (positive y) or down (negative y) by y units.
Mark the spot where you land.

example.problem: Plot the point (3, 2) on a coordinate plane.
example.solution: Start at origin (0, 0). Move 3 units right. Then move 2 units up. Plot the point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plotting is like following directions: first go right/left, then go up/down.

slides.title: Rajesh Practices Plotting
slides.storyContext: Grandmother gives Rajesh five clues. 'Plot these treasures: (1, 2), (−2, 3), (3, −1), (−1, −2), and (0, 0). Mark each one. The one at the origin is the golden coin! The others are gemstones.' Rajesh works methodically, starting at the origin, counting carefully in each direction.
slides.inSimpleWords: Practice plotting by counting: start at (0, 0), move horizontally first, then vertically.

slides.title: Reading a Point from the Graph

points.text: If a point is already plotted, find its coordinates by dropping vertical and horizontal lines to the axes.
The x-coordinate is where the vertical line hits the x-axis.
The y-coordinate is where the horizontal line hits the y-axis.

example.problem: A point is 4 units right of the origin and 2 units up. Write its coordinates.
example.solution: The coordinates are (4, 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: To read a point's coordinates, look where it lines up with the x-axis and y-axis.

image.alt: Reading a Point from the Graph — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Finding Treasures by Reading Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Now Grandmother shows Rajesh a map with treasures already marked as dots. 'These dots are treasures I hid last year. Can you tell me where each one is by reading the coordinates from the map?' Rajesh learns to reverse the process: instead of plotting from coordinates, he reads coordinates from a plot.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you see a plotted point, you can read its coordinates by checking its position relative to both axes.

slides.title: Grandmother's Treasure Locations
slides.storyContext: Grandmother gives Rajesh several clues. The treasure room has treasures at: (2, 3), (−1, 2), (3, −2), and (−2, −3). Plot them and name their quadrants.

example.problem: Plot (2, 3), (−1, 2), (3, −2), (−2, −3). State their quadrants.
example.solution: (2, 3): Quadrant I. (−1, 2): Quadrant II. (3, −2): Quadrant IV. (−2, −3): Quadrant III.

slides.inSimpleWords: By plotting multiple points, you can see patterns and find hidden treasures on a map.

image.alt: Grandmother's Treasure Locations — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: The Grand Challenge
slides.storyContext: Grandmother smiles. 'One final test, beta. I have hidden the greatest treasure—the Family Heirloom Necklace—at a secret location on this map. You must use everything you have learned to find it.' She gives him a grid and a single coordinate: (−4, 4). Rajesh feels the weight of the challenge.
slides.inSimpleWords: A coordinate plane is not just a game—it is a real tool to navigate and find things in the world.

slides.title: Real-World Uses of Coordinates

points.label: Treasure hunts and maps
points.text: Ancient and modern maps use coordinate grids (latitude and longitude) to locate places.

points.label: Video games
points.text: Characters move on coordinate planes—a player's position is stored as (x, y).

points.label: GPS systems
points.text: Every location on Earth is identified by coordinates (latitude, longitude).

points.label: Architecture and construction
points.text: Buildings are designed on coordinate grids to ensure precise placement of rooms and structures.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coordinates are used to pinpoint locations in real life—from maps to games to GPS.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's grandmother says: 'Four treasures are hidden. First, move 5 steps right and 4 steps up. That is clue 1. Clue 2: 3 steps left and 2 steps up. Clue 3: 2 steps right and 5 steps down. Clue 4: 4 steps left and 3 steps down.' Write the ordered pairs for all four treasures.

example.problem: Convert Grandmother's directions to ordered pairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert word clues to coordinates: right/left is x, up/down is y.

image.alt: Can You Solve This? — Another Peek Beyond the Point

slides.title: Rajesh Finds the Heirloom
slides.storyContext: Rajesh carefully places his pencil at the origin. He counts 4 steps left (negative x) and 4 steps up (positive y). He marks the spot: (−4, 4). The coordinate points to a loose tile on Grandmother's floor. He lifts it and finds the necklace! His eyes shine. Grandmother embraces him. 'You have mastered the coordinate plane, beta. Now you can find anything on a map—or navigate anywhere in the world.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you understand coordinates, you can find anything and navigate anywhere using just two numbers.

slides.title: Distance Between Two Points

points.text: Once you have coordinates for two points, you can find the distance between them.
If the points are (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), the distance is √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
This is called the distance formula.

example.problem: Find the distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6).

slides.inSimpleWords: The distance formula uses coordinates to calculate how far apart two points are on a plane.

slides.title: Measuring Between Treasures
slides.storyContext: Rajesh discovers that two treasures are at (2, 3) and (5, 7). 'Grandmother, how far apart are these treasures?' Grandmother smiles and teaches him the distance formula. Rajesh realizes that coordinates do not just tell him where things are—they also tell him how far apart they are.
slides.inSimpleWords: Coordinates help you not only find things but also measure distances between them.

slides.title: Midpoint Between Two Points

points.text: The midpoint is the point exactly halfway between two other points.
If the two points are (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), the midpoint is [(x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2].
You simply average the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates.

example.problem: Find the midpoint between (2, 4) and (8, 10).

slides.inSimpleWords: The midpoint is found by averaging the x and y coordinates of two points.

slides.title: The Meeting Point
slides.storyContext: Rajesh and his friend Priya each hide a treasure: Rajesh at (1, 1) and Priya at (9, 9). They want to meet exactly halfway. Using the midpoint formula, they find the meeting point at (5, 5). They plan to meet there tomorrow!
slides.inSimpleWords: If two people are at different coordinates, the midpoint helps them find where to meet.

slides.title: A Practical Grid Search
slides.storyContext: Rajesh imagines a larger treasure hunt across his village. Treasures are at (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 6), and (0, 6)—the four corners of a square field. What is the center of this field?

example.problem: Find the center (midpoint) of a square with corners at (0, 0) and (6, 6).
example.solution: The center is the midpoint of the diagonal from (0, 0) to (6, 6): [(0+6)/2, (0+6)/2] = (3, 3).

slides.inSimpleWords: The midpoint formula works for any two points, helping you find meeting places or centers of regions.

slides.title: Symmetry on the Coordinate Plane

points.text: Two points are symmetric about the x-axis if they have the same x-coordinate but opposite y-coordinates.
Two points are symmetric about the y-axis if they have the same y-coordinate but opposite x-coordinates.
Example: (3, 4) and (3, −4) are symmetric about the x-axis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry on a coordinate plane means points that are mirror images across an axis.

slides.title: Symmetry in Grandmother's Garden
slides.storyContext: Rajesh plots the positions of trees in Grandmother's garden on a coordinate plane. He notices that some trees are placed symmetrically—if one tree is at (2, 3), another is at (2, −3) on the opposite side of the x-axis! This symmetry makes the garden beautiful and balanced.
slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetric arrangements are pleasing to the eye and often appear in nature and design.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: The coordinate plane has an x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical) that meet at the origin (0, 0).
An ordered pair (x, y) specifies a point's location.
The four quadrants are determined by positive/negative x and y.
To plot a point: start at origin, move x units horizontally, then y units vertically.
To read a point's coordinates: drop lines to both axes.
Distance formula and midpoint formula extend coordinate skills to measure and find meeting points.

slides.inSimpleWords: The coordinate plane is like a map grid—ordered pairs tell you exactly where to find things, and formulas help you measure and navigate.

image.alt: What We Learned — Another Peek Beyond the Point

subject: Mathematics
title: The City Graph
hook: Meera plots bus routes on a grid, creating a linear graph that shows relationships between distance and time.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: class-7 student curious about real-world math

slides.title: The City Graph
slides.storyContext: Meera watches buses move through Mumbai and learns how to graph motion and relationships.

slides.title: The Bus Route
slides.storyContext: Uncle runs a bus company in Mumbai. He shows Meera a chart: 'Look, beta. At time 0, the bus is at kilometer 0. After 1 hour, it is at kilometer 50. After 2 hours, it is at kilometer 100.' Meera sees a pattern. 'The distance increases by 50 every hour!' Uncle smiles. 'Exactly! That is a linear relationship. Let me show you how to graph it.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When two quantities change together in a steady pattern, their relationship is linear and forms a straight line on a graph.

slides.title: Variables and Relationships

points.text: Two quantities that change together have a relationship.
The independent variable is what we control or what happens first (usually time, x).
The dependent variable depends on the independent variable (usually distance, y).
In the bus example: time is independent (x), distance is dependent (y).

example.problem: A bus travels 50 km per hour. Distance depends on time. Which is the independent variable?
example.solution: Time is independent (x). Distance is dependent (y) because it depends on how long we travel.

slides.inSimpleWords: One variable causes a change in the other—that second one is dependent.

slides.title: Meera Watches a Bus
slides.storyContext: Meera sits on the platform and watches a bus leave the station. Every hour, the bus travels exactly 50 km. 'So if I plot time on the bottom and distance on the side, I get a straight line!' Meera sketches on paper, plotting points for 0 hours, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 3 hours.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you plot pairs of connected values (time and distance, or x and y), you create a graph that shows the relationship.

slides.title: Tables and Patterns

points.text: Before graphing, you can organize x and y values in a table.
Look for patterns: does y increase by the same amount each time x increases?
If yes, the relationship is linear.

example.problem: Make a table for the bus: time (hours) and distance (km) for times 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
example.solution: Time: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Distance: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200. The distance increases by 50 for each hour—linear!

slides.inSimpleWords: A table helps you spot patterns before you draw a graph.

slides.title: Linear Equations

points.text: A linear equation describes a relationship that forms a straight line.
The simplest form is y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept.
For the bus: distance = 50 × time, or y = 50x (b = 0 because the bus starts at 0 km).

example.problem: The bus travels at 50 km/hour starting from 0 km. Write the equation.
example.solution: y = 50x, where y is distance (km) and x is time (hours).

slides.inSimpleWords: A linear equation uses y and x to show how one quantity depends on another.

slides.title: Uncle Explains the Formula
slides.storyContext: Uncle draws on a whiteboard: 'y = 50x. What does this mean? y is the distance we want to find. 50 is how fast the bus travels—every hour, it goes 50 km. x is the time in hours. And there is no plus b because the bus starts at zero distance.' Meera nods. 'So if x = 3, then y = 50 times 3, which is 150 km!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The equation y = mx + b is a recipe: m is the speed, b is the starting point, and x is the input.

slides.title: Slope

points.text: Slope measures how steep a line is—how much y changes for every unit change in x.
Slope = (change in y) / (change in x) = rise / run.
In the bus route: for every 1 hour (x), distance (y) increases by 50 km. Slope = 50.
A positive slope means y increases as x increases. A negative slope means y decreases as x increases.

example.problem: If a bus is at 50 km after 1 hour and 100 km after 2 hours, what is the slope?

slides.inSimpleWords: Slope tells you how fast the dependent variable changes as the independent variable changes.

slides.title: Comparing Two Bus Routes
slides.storyContext: Meera realizes that not all buses travel at the same speed. Uncle shows her two routes: Route A goes 50 km/hour, and Route B goes 40 km/hour. 'Both are straight lines, but Route A is steeper because it travels faster.' Meera sketches both lines. She sees that a steeper line means a bigger slope, which means faster change.
slides.inSimpleWords: A steeper line means a larger slope—faster change. A gentle line means a smaller slope—slower change.

slides.title: Y-Intercept

points.text: The y-intercept is the value of y when x is 0 (where the line crosses the y-axis).
In y = 50x, the y-intercept is 0 (the bus starts at 0 km).
In y = 2x + 5, the y-intercept is 5.
The y-intercept tells you the starting point or initial value.

example.problem: A bus route: y = 40x + 10. What is the y-intercept, and what does it mean?
example.solution: The y-intercept is 10. It means the bus started 10 km away from the origin point.

slides.inSimpleWords: The y-intercept is the starting value when x equals zero.

slides.title: A Bus with a Head Start
slides.storyContext: Uncle points to a new bus route. 'This bus started 20 km away from the main station and then travels at 60 km/hour. The equation is y = 60x + 20. See? The +20 is where the bus started!' Meera understands. 'So even at time 0, the bus is not at 0 km; it is at 20 km!'
slides.inSimpleWords: If a bus or any line does not start at zero, the y-intercept tells you where it starts.

slides.title: Plotting a Linear Graph

points.text: To plot a line, find at least two points and draw a straight line through them.
Use the y-intercept (0, b) as your first point.
Use the slope to find a second point: move right 1 unit (or any distance), then up by the slope.
Example: y = 2x + 1. Start at (0, 1). Move 1 right, 2 up to (1, 3). Draw the line.

example.problem: Plot the line y = 3x. Find two points and draw the line.
example.solution: Point 1: (0, 0). Point 2: (1, 3). Draw a straight line through both.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plot two points using the equation, then connect them with a straight line.

slides.title: Meera Plots the Bus Route
slides.storyContext: Meera carefully draws a coordinate plane on graph paper. For the route y = 50x, she marks (0, 0). Then she counts right 1 hour and up 50 km to mark (1, 50). She draws a straight line through both points. 'Look, Uncle! The line shows the entire trip!' Uncle nods proudly.
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you plot two points, you can draw the entire line—and it shows the complete pattern for all time values.

slides.title: Reading Values from a Graph

points.text: Once a line is plotted, you can read any y-value by finding a point on the line at a given x-value.
Find x on the horizontal axis, go up to the line, then read the y-value on the vertical axis.
This is called 'using the graph to predict or find values'.

example.problem: For the route y = 50x, what distance has the bus traveled after 2.5 hours? Use the graph.
example.solution: Find x = 2.5 on the horizontal axis, go up to the line, read y = 125 km.

slides.inSimpleWords: A graph lets you find the answer to 'if x is this, what is y?' without doing the math again.

slides.title: Uncle's Bus Schedule
slides.storyContext: Uncle's bus leaves Mumbai at 6 AM. After t hours, the bus is at distance d = 60t + 20 (in km, the +20 is because it started 20 km out of the city). Plot this relationship for 0 to 5 hours.

example.problem: Graph d = 60t + 20 for t = 0 to 5.
example.solution: t=0: d=20. t=1: d=80. t=2: d=140. t=3: d=200. t=4: d=260. t=5: d=320. Plot these points and draw a straight line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Build a table of x and y values from the equation, plot them, and connect with a line.

slides.title: Finding When the Bus Arrives
slides.storyContext: Meera's friend lives 200 km away. She asks Uncle, 'When will the bus reach my house?' Using the equation y = 60x + 20, Uncle rearranges: 200 = 60x + 20. So 180 = 60x, and x = 3. 'The bus will arrive in 3 hours!' Using algebra and graphs together makes the answer clear.
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear equations help you answer real questions: how long until arrival, how far after time x, or what time for distance y.

slides.title: Non-Linear vs. Linear Relationships

points.label: Linear
points.text: A straight line on the graph. Both variables change at a constant rate.

points.label: Non-linear
points.text: A curved line on the graph. The rate of change is not constant—it speeds up or slows down.

points.label: Example of non-linear
points.text: A ball thrown in the air follows a curved path (parabola) because gravity accelerates it downward.

slides.inSimpleWords: If the graph is a straight line, the relationship is linear. If it curves, the relationship is non-linear.

slides.title: A Train That Accelerates
slides.storyContext: Meera learns that a different vehicle—a train—accelerates, meaning it goes faster and faster. Its distance equation is y = x². When Meera plots this, it forms a curve, not a line! 'This is not linear!' she exclaims. Uncle smiles. 'Right, beta. Not everything in the world is linear. But buses traveling at constant speed? That is linear.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear relationships are steady and constant. Real-world motion often curves because of acceleration or deceleration.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Meera receives two bus routes: Bus A follows y = 40x (starting at 0 km). Bus B follows y = 30x + 50 (starting 50 km away). After 2 hours, which bus is farther? Graph both lines on the same coordinate plane.

example.problem: At t=2, where is each bus? Plot both routes for t=0 to 4.
example.solution: Bus A at t=2: y=40(2)=80 km. Bus B at t=2: y=30(2)+50=110 km. Bus B is farther. Plot both lines: A goes through (0,0) and (2,80). B goes through (0,50) and (2,110).

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare two linear relationships by plotting both lines and reading their values.

slides.title: Meera Teaches Her Parents
slides.storyContext: At dinner, Meera explains everything to her parents. She draws graphs showing bus routes, slopes, and y-intercepts. 'See? These straight lines tell us when buses arrive, how far they travel, and how fast they go!' Her parents are amazed. 'Our daughter is a mathematician!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear graphs and equations are powerful tools for understanding and predicting real-world motion.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

points.label: Parallel lines
points.text: Two lines with the same slope never cross. y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x + 5 are parallel (both slope = 2).

points.label: Perpendicular lines
points.text: Two lines whose slopes multiply to give −1 cross at a right angle. y = 2x and y = −½x are perpendicular.

example.problem: Are y = 3x + 2 and y = 3x − 5 parallel or perpendicular?
example.solution: Both have slope 3, so they are parallel. They never meet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular lines' slopes multiply to −1.

slides.title: Two Parallel Bus Routes
slides.storyContext: Meera notices that two buses on the same schedule travel at the same speed but start from different stations. Their routes are parallel! 'If Bus A is always faster than Bus B at every point in time, but they travel at the same speed, they will never meet. That is what parallel means!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Two buses with the same speed are parallel routes—they stay the same distance apart forever.

slides.title: Slope-Intercept Form Practice
slides.storyContext: Meera practices identifying slopes and y-intercepts from equations. For y = 3x + 7, she quickly says: 'Slope = 3, y-intercept = 7.' For y = −2x + 4, she says: 'Slope = −2, y-intercept = 4. This line goes down!'

example.problem: For y = −5x + 15, identify the slope and y-intercept.
example.solution: Slope = −5, y-intercept = 15. The line has a negative slope (goes downward) and crosses the y-axis at (0, 15).

slides.inSimpleWords: In y = mx + b, m is always the slope and b is always the y-intercept.

slides.title: Writing Linear Equations from Two Points

points.text: If you know two points on a line, you can write its equation.
Step 1: Calculate slope m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁).
Step 2: Use one point and m to find b: y = mx + b.
Step 3: Write the equation y = mx + b.

example.problem: Write the equation of a line through points (1, 3) and (3, 7).
example.solution: Slope m = (7 − 3)/(3 − 1) = 4/2 = 2. Using point (1, 3): 3 = 2(1) + b, so b = 1. Equation: y = 2x + 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: With two points, you can always find the slope and y-intercept, then write the equation.

slides.title: Real-World Graphing
slides.storyContext: Meera realizes that linear graphs are everywhere. The phone bill depends linearly on minutes used. Electricity costs depend on kilowatt-hours. Temperature trends follow linear patterns over time. Every real-world relationship that changes at a constant rate can be graphed as a line.
slides.inSimpleWords: Linear relationships appear throughout the real world—any steady change can be graphed as a straight line.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A linear equation (y = mx + b) describes a relationship that forms a straight line.
Slope (m) is the rate of change—how much y changes per unit of x.
The y-intercept (b) is the starting value when x is 0.
To plot a line, find at least two points and connect them.
Linear graphs model real-world relationships like bus routes, temperature changes, and business profits.
Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular lines cross at right angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear graphs show steady relationships—straight lines with a slope and a starting point. They help us understand and predict real-world motion.

image.alt: What We Learned — Connecting the Dots...

subject: Mathematics
title: Anvi's Tile Design Challenge
hook: Help a young architect design perfect tiles for her village festival stage using straightedges and compasses.

characters.name: Anvi
characters.role: geometry-loving student who dreams of designing buildings

characters.name: Rohan
characters.role: Anvi's friend who helps with the design project

slides.title: Constructions and Tilings: Anvi's Tile Design Challenge
The Festival Stage
slides.storyContext: Anvi's village is hosting Diwali celebrations, and the temple committee wants a beautiful tiled stage. Anvi volunteers to design the tile pattern, but there's a catch: she has only a straightedge (unmarked ruler) and a compass—no measuring tape. Guru Ramesh, the carpenter, says, "Geometry solves this. You don't need numbers; you need clever construction." Rohan watches eagerly as they begin.

slides.title: What Is a Geometric Construction?
slides.storyContext: Guru Ramesh opens his toolbox. "A construction," he explains, "is drawing shapes exactly—no guessing, no measuring with numbers. Only two tools: the straightedge to draw straight lines, and the compass to copy distances and draw circles."

points.label: Definition
points.text: A geometric construction uses only a straightedge and compass to create shapes with exact relationships (like equal sides or equal angles).

points.label: Why it matters
points.text: Architects and builders use constructions to scale designs from small to large without errors. In Anvi's case, she can construct the tile shape once, then repeat it perfectly.

slides.inSimpleWords: A construction is drawing a perfect shape using only a straight edge and compass—no numbers, no guessing.

slides.title: Anvi Learns the Compass
slides.storyContext: Guru Ramesh hands Anvi a compass. 'Watch. The needle point stays fixed, and the pencil arm draws a circle at a fixed distance. This radius can be copied—if I mark the distance between two points with the compass, I can draw an arc of the same distance anywhere else.' Rohan experiments and successfully draws two identical arcs. 'This is like copying with a photocopy machine!'
slides.inSimpleWords: A compass copies distances perfectly—you can use the same distance again and again without measuring.

slides.title: The Straightedge and Compass: Tools of Precision

points.text: A straightedge has no markings—it only draws straight lines, not measurements.
A compass has two legs: one sharp point (for the center) and one with pencil (for drawing).
Together, they can create any regular polygon if you know the techniques.

slides.inSimpleWords: These two simple tools are all you need to draw perfect shapes—no numbers, no measuring.

slides.title: Constructing an Equilateral Triangle
slides.storyContext: "Our tiles will be equilateral triangles," says Guru Ramesh. "That means all three sides are equal, and all angles are 60°. Watch how the compass does the work."

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Draw a line segment AB with the straightedge.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Place the compass point at A, open it to length AB, and draw an arc above the line.

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Without changing the compass width, place the point at B and draw another arc that crosses the first arc at point C.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Join A to C and B to C with the straightedge. Triangle ABC is equilateral.

example.problem: If AB = 5 cm, what can you say about AC and BC?
example.solution: AC = BC = AB = 5 cm because the compass kept the same width for all three arcs. All three sides equal means an equilateral triangle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use a compass to copy the distance, then draw two arcs that meet. Connect the points and you have a perfect triangle with all sides equal.

image.alt: Constructing an Equilateral Triangle — Constructions and Tilings

slides.title: Anvi Constructs Her First Triangle
slides.storyContext: Anvi draws a line segment for the base. She sets the compass to the length of this base and draws arcs from both ends. Where they meet, she marks point C. Connecting all three points, she has a perfect equilateral triangle! 'Guru Ramesh, I made it!' He smiles. 'And it has no numbers, just geometry.'
slides.inSimpleWords: An equilateral triangle has all sides equal and all angles 60 degrees—it is the most symmetric triangle.

slides.title: Constructing Another Triangle
slides.storyContext: Anvi practices by constructing a second equilateral triangle of a different size. She draws a longer base and repeats the compass technique. Soon she has two perfect triangles—one large, one small—and both are equilateral!

example.problem: Construct an equilateral triangle with a base of 3 cm using only compass and straightedge.
example.solution: Draw base AB = 3 cm. Open compass to 3 cm, place at A, draw arc. Place at B (same radius), draw arc that intersects first arc at C. Join A-C and B-C. Triangle ABC is equilateral with all sides = 3 cm and all angles = 60°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you learn the technique, you can construct perfect equilateral triangles of any size.

slides.title: Constructing a Square
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks, "What if we want square tiles instead?" Guru Ramesh nods. "Good question. A square is trickier because we need right angles. Let me show you."

points.label: Method
points.text: Draw a line segment AB. At point A, construct a perpendicular using the compass and straightedge (using the property that a perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the circle's center). Mark point D on this perpendicular such that AD = AB. Similarly, mark C so that BC = AB and angle D = angle C = 90°. Join D to C.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The compass ensures all sides are equal; the perpendicular ensures all angles are 90°.

slides.inSimpleWords: To build a square, first draw a line, then use compass arcs to create a perpendicular line of equal length, then complete the square.

image.alt: Constructing a Square — Constructions and Tilings

slides.title: Creating a Perpendicular
slides.storyContext: Guru Ramesh demonstrates. 'To make a right angle without a protractor, I need perpendicularity. I draw a line, then use the compass to find a point equidistant from two points on the line. That gives me a perpendicular.' Anvi watches closely as he executes each step. The perpendicular line is perfect, without any guessing.
slides.inSimpleWords: A perpendicular line is at a right angle (90 degrees). You can construct it using only a compass and straightedge.

slides.title: Bisecting an Angle
slides.storyContext: "Sometimes," Guru Ramesh continues, "we need to split an angle exactly in half. The compass can do that too."

points.label: Goal
points.text: To bisect (split) angle AOB into two equal angles.

points.label: Steps
points.text: 1. Place compass at O, draw an arc that crosses both rays OA and OB. Mark these points P and Q. 2. Place compass at P and Q (with the same radius), draw two arcs that intersect at a point M. 3. Draw ray OM. This ray bisects angle AOB.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The compass arcs create equal distances, so triangle OPM is congruent to triangle OQM, making angle POM = angle QOM.

slides.inSimpleWords: To split an angle in half, use the compass to draw equal arcs from both sides of the angle, then find where they cross.

image.alt: Bisecting an Angle — Constructions and Tilings

slides.title: Bisecting for Beauty
slides.storyContext: Anvi thinks about her design. 'If I bisect angles, I can divide shapes into smaller, equal parts! That would create symmetric patterns!' Guru Ramesh nods. 'Yes, beta. Many beautiful patterns come from bisecting angles and constructing symmetric shapes.'
slides.inSimpleWords: By bisecting angles and copying distances, you can create complex, symmetric, beautiful patterns.

slides.title: What Are Tilings (Tessellations)?
slides.storyContext: Anvi sketches triangles on paper. "Look, Guru—if I repeat these triangles, they fit together with no gaps or overlaps!" Guru Ramesh smiles. "That's tiling, or tessellation. Nature does this all the time."

points.label: Definition
points.text: A tiling is a pattern where shapes fit together to cover a flat surface completely, with no gaps or overlaps.

points.label: Key fact
points.text: The interior angles of shapes that meet at each point must sum to exactly 360°.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Equilateral triangles (60° each; six fit at a point: 6 × 60° = 360°), squares (90° each; four fit: 4 × 90° = 360°), regular hexagons (120° each; three fit: 3 × 120° = 360°).

example.problem: Can you tile a floor with regular pentagons (each interior angle = 108°)?
example.solution: No. If you try to place pentagons at a point: 108° + 108° + 108° = 324°. The fourth corner leaves a gap of 36°. Pentagons don't tile the plane.

slides.inSimpleWords: A tiling is when shapes fit together like a puzzle with no gaps. The angles at every corner point must add up to 360°.

slides.title: Testing the Angle Rule
slides.storyContext: Rohan cuts out several cardboard equilateral triangles from Anvi's construction. Each angle is 60°. He arranges six triangles around a central point. 'They fit perfectly with no gaps!' Anvi calculates: '6 times 60 equals 360! The angles add up exactly!' She realizes this is why triangles tile so beautifully.
slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes tile perfectly when their angles around a point add up to exactly 360 degrees.

slides.title: Interior Angles of Regular Polygons

points.text: An equilateral triangle has three 60° angles.
A square has four 90° angles.
A regular pentagon has five 108° angles.
A regular hexagon has six 120° angles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each regular polygon has equal interior angles, and the sum depends on the number of sides.

slides.title: Regular Tilings
slides.storyContext: "There are only three perfect tilings," Guru Ramesh explains. "And nature chose all three for a reason."

points.label: Triangular tiling
points.text: Equilateral triangles (6 per point). Bees use this in honeycombs—maximizes space for honey!

points.label: Square tiling
points.text: Squares (4 per point). This tiles the simplest way—floors, tiles, checkerboards.

points.label: Hexagonal tiling
points.text: Regular hexagons (3 per point). Honeycombs again! Hexagons are nature's answer for strength and efficiency.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only three regular shapes tile perfectly: triangles, squares, and hexagons. Bees know this and use hexagons in their hives!

slides.title: Anvi Chooses Triangles for Her Stage
slides.storyContext: Anvi decides on triangular tiles. 'Triangles fit together perfectly, and six meet at every corner. It will be strong and beautiful!' She constructs one perfect equilateral triangle and makes a stencil. Now she can repeat it as many times as needed for the stage.
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you construct one perfect tile shape, you can copy it many times to cover any area.

slides.title: Anvi's Tile Design
slides.storyContext: Anvi decides on a hexagonal tiling for the stage—it's beautiful and strong. "If the hexagon has a side of 1 meter," she calculates, "then I can construct each tile with the compass, and repeat it across the entire stage."

example.problem: Anvi constructs a regular hexagon with side length 1 meter using only a compass and straightedge. If the stage is 6 meters × 6 meters, how many complete hexagons can she fit along one edge (assuming no gaps)?
example.solution: A regular hexagon with side 1 meter has a 'width' (distance across flats) of approximately √3 ≈ 1.73 meters. So along a 6-meter edge, she can fit about 6 ÷ 1.73 ≈ 3 to 4 hexagons, depending on orientation. The exact number depends on how she arranges them—hexagonal tiling lets her nestle them efficiently.

slides.title: The Grand Pattern
slides.storyContext: Anvi and Rohan carefully place triangular tiles on the stage. Each triangle is identical, constructed using Anvi's compass and straightedge technique. The pattern is flawless—no gaps, no overlaps. Village members gather, amazed at the precision and beauty. 'This is mathematics in action!' says Guru Ramesh.
slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect constructions and correct tiling rules create beautiful, precise patterns that last for generations.

slides.title: Semi-Regular Tilings (Archimedean Tilings)

points.text: Beyond the three regular tilings, there are tilings using combinations of regular shapes.
Example: a tiling of triangles and squares together (in a specific pattern) can tile the plane.
The key is still that angles around every point must sum to exactly 360°.

example.problem: Can a pattern of triangles (60°) and squares (90°) tile the plane?
example.solution: Yes, if arranged correctly: 2 triangles (120°) + 1 square (90°) + another square (90°) + half another shape... Actually, yes: 2 triangles + 2 squares = 120° + 180° = 300°, so we need 60° more = 1 triangle. One valid arrangement uses 4 triangles and 2 squares at some points.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can mix shapes in tilings as long as the angles around each point add up to 360 degrees.

slides.title: Anvi's Next Challenge
slides.storyContext: The village elder approaches Anvi. 'Your triangle pattern is beautiful! But the next temple has a larger stage. Can you design a pattern using two different shapes?' Anvi thinks hard. 'I can combine squares and triangles if the angles add up to 360°!' Guru Ramesh smiles. 'That is the mark of a true mathematician, beta.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you master single-shape tilings, you can combine shapes to create even more complex and beautiful patterns.

slides.title: Why Only Three Regular Tilings?

points.text: A tiling works only if interior angles at each point sum to 360°.
Equilateral triangles: 6 × 60° = 360°. ✓
Pentagons: 108° × 3 = 324°; 108° × 4 = 432°. Neither works!

slides.inSimpleWords: Only three regular polygons can tile because their angles happen to divide 360° evenly.

slides.title: Your Challenge: Design a Tile Pattern
slides.storyContext: Now it's your turn. You have only a straightedge and compass.

example.problem: Can you construct a regular octagon (8-sided shape, each interior angle = 135°)? If yes, describe the steps. If no, explain why not using angle arithmetic.
example.solution: This is difficult with only compass and straightedge (unlike triangles and squares). A regular octagon requires special constructions involving angle trisection, which is NOT possible with compass and straightedge alone (a classical math fact). However, you CAN construct an octagon by cutting off the corners of a square: draw a square, then construct 45° angles at each corner (by bisecting 90°), and cut off the corners. This creates an octagon that tiles with squares.

slides.title: Timeless Beauty
slides.storyContext: Years later, travelers visit the village and marvel at the perfectly tiled stage. 'How did they make this without modern tools?' they ask. Anvi, now a young architect, smiles. 'With a straightedge, a compass, and the wisdom of geometry. The same techniques have been used for thousands of years.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Geometric constructions are timeless—the same methods used in ancient times still create perfect shapes today.

slides.title: Nature's Tilings: Hidden Patterns

points.text: Honeycombs use hexagonal tilings—the most efficient way to store honey and protect the colony.
Turtle shells and pinecones show triangular and spiral tilings found in nature.
Dragonfly wings and butterfly patterns often reflect geometric tessellations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nature discovered tiling millions of years before humans—bees, tortoises, and insects all use perfect geometric patterns.

points.text: Geometric constructions use only straightedge and compass—no numbers needed—to create shapes with exact relationships.
Key constructions: equilateral triangles, squares, angle bisectors.
Tilings (tessellations) are patterns where shapes fit together with no gaps or overlaps.
The angles at any meeting point in a tiling must sum to exactly 360°.
Only three regular shapes tile perfectly: equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons.
Real-world use: architects, tile makers, and bees use tilings for strength, beauty, and efficiency.
